units.translation: where πόρον [a passage] M: but πόρους [passages] in Dionysius A.R. 7, 36 and others indicated in the annotation.
Τίν᾽ ἂν πόρον τέμνοιν γά-μου [What passage of marriage might they cut?]
as it is now read from the apograph for πόνος [toil].
with devices he yoked the strait of Helle, so as to have a passage
and the pure air, the path of birds
of a long journey — a passage
do not, by spreading garments, make a passage that invites envy
the one who gives, making paths that are spiritless and birdless
for thick and shadowy paths of the mind stretch out
to guard the sailing out and the sea-resounding passages
and may they rescue their friends from the paths of the sea
he crosses through the ice-bound passage
the circle of the sun passed through the middle of its course
and around the broad passage of Helle
from father Ocean, the unquenchable stream
around the stream of Pluto's passage
and he does not allow crossing the Ismenian passage
to the passage of the Axius
not having crossed the passage of the river Halys
beside the passage of the Scamander
and all the paths going from one road
around the stream of Triton, the ancestral passage
for he is clever at finding passages even from impossible situations
he has appeared as a teacher of every art to mortals and a great resource
what arts and resources I devised
What passage of marriage might they cut?

The letter α θυμ προδυχατυρ [the letter alpha with the theta?] makes it clear that the present is not πορπάζω [to fasten with a pin], but πορπάω [to fasten with a pin], whence the aorist πορπῆσαι [to fasten with a pin]. But the tragedians seem to have preferred the Doric form, as Euripides said πόρπαμα [a pin], not πόρπημα [a pin]: b. Thes. vol. 6 p. 1501. On this kind in general Lobeck ad Phryn. p. 205, to whose examples perhaps should be added αὔδασον [speak!] in a trimeter of Euripides Phoen. 125.
and now fasten this securely with a pin
